source.text: אִ֛ישׁ הָיָ֥ה בְאֶֽרֶץ־ע֖וּץ אִיּ֣וֹב שְׁמ֑וֹ וְהָיָ֣ה׀הָאִ֣ישׁ הַה֗וּא תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר וִירֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֥ר מֵרָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: A man there was in [the] land of Uz, Job [was] his name; and was the man that blameless and upright, and fearing God and turning aside from evil.

en.L: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job; and that man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God and turned away from evil.
en.B: There was a man in the land of Uz named Job. He was blameless and upright; he feared God and turned away from evil.
en.R: There was once a man named Job who lived in the land of Uz. He was blameless and upright. He honored God and kept away from evil.

decisions.choice: the land of Uz: a land east of Israel; Job is not an Israelite
decisions.reason: Uz is a name linked both with Aram (Genesis 10:23; 22:21) and with Edom (Genesis 36:28; Lamentations 4:21, "daughter of Edom, who lives in the land of Uz"), so it lay somewhere to the east or southeast of Israel; its exact place is not known. The story is set outside Israel, gives no date, and never mentions Israel's history, law or temple. Job and his friends are wise men of the East (1:3; 2:11).

decisions.choice: blameless and upright: whole in character and straight in conduct, not sinless
decisions.reason: The first word describes what is whole and complete, with nothing lacking; of a person it means integrity, a life that is all of one piece (Genesis 25:27; Psalm 37:37). Its noun is the "integrity" Job holds fast to (2:3, 9; 27:5; 31:6), and the question of the whole book is whether that integrity is real. The second word means straight, honest, doing what is right. Neither word claims that Job never sinned: he offers sacrifices in case of sin (1:5) and later speaks of the sins of his youth (13:26). God repeats the same description (1:8; 2:3).

decisions.choice: feared God and turned away from evil: reverent obedience to God
decisions.reason: To fear God is to hold him in awe and so to obey him; it is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10), and Job 28:28 joins the same two phrases: "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding". The participles describe Job's settled way of life, not a single act.

decisions.choice: blameless and upright at every level
alternatives: honest and did what was right (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Blameless" is the book's theme word; keeping it at every level lets Readable readers hear it again at 1:8, 2:3 and in Job's speeches. Readable keeps "upright" beside it, as the fixed pair of the Hebrew.

decisions.choice: honored God; kept away from evil (Readable)
decisions.reason: For a new reader "feared God" can sound like terror. Readable says "honored God", the respect and obedience the phrase means; Literal and Balanced keep "feared God".

source.text: וַיִּוָּ֥לְדוּ ל֛וֹ שִׁבְעָ֥ה בָנִ֖ים וְשָׁל֥וֹשׁ בָּנֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: And were born to him seven sons and three daughters.

en.L: And there were born to him seven sons and three daughters.
en.B: He had seven sons and three daughters.
en.R: He had seven sons and three daughters.

decisions.choice: seven sons and three daughters: a complete and blessed family
decisions.reason: Many sons were counted a sign of God's blessing (Psalm 127:3-5; Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 2:5). Seven and three, which add up to ten, are numbers of fullness, and the same numbers of children are given to Job again at the end (42:13). The numbers of his flocks in the next verse follow the same pattern.

decisions.choice: He had (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "there were born to him", which Literal keeps; Balanced and Readable use the plain English way of saying it.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י מִ֠קְנֵהוּ שִֽׁבְעַ֨ת אַלְפֵי־צֹ֜אן וּשְׁלֹ֧שֶׁת אַלְפֵ֣י גְמַלִּ֗ים וַחֲמֵ֨שׁ מֵא֤וֹת צֶֽמֶד־בָּקָר֙ וַחֲמֵ֣שׁ מֵא֣וֹת אֲתוֹנ֔וֹת וַעֲבֻדָּ֖ה רַבָּ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד וַיְהִי֙ הָאִ֣ישׁ הַה֔וּא גָּד֖וֹל מִכָּל־בְּנֵי־קֶֽדֶם׃

records.literal_gloss: And was his livestock seven thousand(s) [of] sheep and three thousand(s) [of] camels and five hundred yoke[s] of oxen and five hundred female donkeys, and service [was] very much; and was the man that great more than all [the] sons of [the] east.

en.L: And his livestock was 7,000 sheep and 3,000 camels and 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants; and that man was greater than all the sons of the east.
en.B: He owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys, and he had a great many servants. He was the greatest man among all the peoples of the East.
en.R: He owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 pairs of oxen and 500 female donkeys. He also had a great many servants. He was the richest and most important man in all the lands to the east.

decisions.choice: a rich herdsman's wealth: flocks, camels, plow oxen and donkeys
decisions.reason: Wealth in the ancient East was counted in animals. The word for "sheep" covers the flock, sheep and goats together. Oxen were counted by the yoke, the pair that plows together (1:14), and female donkeys were prized for breeding and milk. Seven and three thousand repeat the numbers of his children (1:2); the totals are doubled at the end (42:12).

decisions.choice: very many servants
decisions.reason: The word means service or work, and here, as in Genesis 26:14, it stands for the people who do the work: a large household of servants. It completes the picture of a great estate.

decisions.choice: the sons of the east: the peoples living east of Israel, toward the desert
decisions.reason: The phrase names the peoples of the lands east of the Jordan and the Syrian-Arabian desert (Genesis 29:1; Judges 6:3). They were known for their wisdom (1 Kings 5:10, numbered 4:30 in many Bibles). "Great" includes wealth and standing together.

decisions.choice: pairs of oxen; the richest and most important (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Yoke" as a count is unfamiliar to many readers, so Readable says "pairs". It spells out "great" as both wealth and standing, which the verse's list of possessions shows.

source.text: וְהָלְכ֤וּ בָנָיו֙ וְעָשׂ֣וּ מִשְׁתֶּ֔ה בֵּ֖ית אִ֣ישׁ יוֹמ֑וֹ וְשָׁלְח֗וּ וְקָרְאוּ֙ לִשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אַחְיֽוֹתֵיהֶ֔ם לֶאֱכֹ֥ל וְלִשְׁתּ֖וֹת עִמָּהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And went his sons and made a feast [at the] house of each one [on] his day, and they sent and called to [the] three of their sisters to eat and to drink with them.

en.L: And his sons would go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and to drink with them.
en.B: His sons used to take turns holding a feast, each in his own house on his day, and they would send for their three sisters and invite them to eat and drink with them.
en.R: Job's sons took turns holding feasts in their homes, each on his own day. They would invite their three sisters to come and eat and drink with them.

decisions.choice: would go and hold: a regular custom, not one event
decisions.reason: The verbs have the form Hebrew narrative uses for what happened again and again (as also in 1:5). The verse describes the family's way of life before the disasters: the brothers met in turn and included their sisters.

decisions.choice: on his day: each son's turn, perhaps his birthday
decisions.reason: "His day" most likely means the day each son's turn came round. In 3:1 "his day" is Job's birthday, so some take it here as each son's birthday, which would make the feasts spread through the year. The text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: a feast: a banquet with drinking
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb "to drink" and names a festive meal with wine (1:13; Esther 1:3; Judges 14:10). The feasting itself is not condemned; it is the setting for Job's care in the next verse.

decisions.choice: used to take turns; took turns (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "take turns" to make clear what "each on his day" means; Literal keeps the Hebrew's "would go and hold a feast".

source.text: וַיְהִ֡י כִּ֣י הִקִּיפֽוּ֩ יְמֵ֨י הַמִּשְׁתֶּ֜ה וַיִּשְׁלַ֧ח אִיּ֣וֹב וַֽיְקַדְּשֵׁ֗ם וְהִשְׁכִּ֣ים בַּבֹּקֶר֮ וְהֶעֱלָ֣ה עֹלוֹת֮ מִסְפַּ֣ר כֻּלָּם֒ כִּ֚י אָמַ֣ר אִיּ֔וֹב אוּלַי֙ חָטְא֣וּ בָנַ֔י וּבֵרֲכ֥וּ אֱלֹהִ֖ים בִּלְבָבָ֑ם כָּ֛כָה יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה אִיּ֖וֹב כָּל־הַיָּמִֽים׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And it was when had gone round [the] days of the feast, and sent Job and sanctified them, and rose early in the morning and offered up burnt offerings [according to the] number of all of them; for said Job, perhaps have sinned my sons and blessed God in their heart. Thus did Job all the days.

en.L: And it was, when the days of feasting had gone their round, that Job would send and consecrate them; and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." This is what Job did all the days.
en.B: Whenever a round of feasting was over, Job would send for his children and consecrate them. He would get up early in the morning and offer a burnt offering for each one of them, because Job said to himself, "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." This is what Job always did.
en.R: When each round of feasts was over, Job would send for his children and make them ready to worship God. Early in the morning he would offer a burnt offering for each of them. Job thought, "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." Job always did this.

decisions.choice: cursed God: the verb is "bless", used in place of "curse"
decisions.reason: The Hebrew verb here is the ordinary word for "bless", but the sense is its opposite: Job fears his children have cursed God, a sin that would call for sacrifice. Writers and scribes avoided putting the words "curse God" into the text, and wrote "bless" instead; the same substitution is made in 1 Kings 21:10, 13, where Naboth is falsely accused of having "blessed" God and the king, a crime punished by death. Job uses it in this sense in 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9 as well. Since the same verb can also be said when taking leave of someone (Genesis 47:10), a few have read it as "said goodbye to God", but "curse" fits every use in the prologue. Where the verb is a real blessing (1:10, 21; 42:12) the context makes it plain.

decisions.choice: consecrate them and offer burnt offerings: Job acts as priest of his household
decisions.reason: To consecrate people is to make them ritually ready to come before God, usually by washing and setting themselves apart (Exodus 19:10, 14; 1 Samuel 16:5). The head of the family then offered the sacrifices himself, as Noah and Abraham did (Genesis 8:20; 22:13), with no priest or sanctuary mentioned. A burnt offering was wholly burned on the altar (Leviticus 1).

decisions.choice: my children: sons and daughters
decisions.reason: The plural of "son" often means children of both sexes (Genesis 30:1). The daughters ate and drank at the feasts too (1:4), and Job offers sacrifices "according to the number of them all", so he most likely has all ten in mind.

decisions.choice: Job did this all the days: his regular practice
decisions.reason: The verb form describes repeated action, and "all the days" means always. Job's care reaches even to sins of the heart that no one could see; the narrator shows this before the test begins.

decisions.choice: Job said (Literal); said to himself (Balanced); thought (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew verb "say" often means to say to oneself, to think (Genesis 20:11). Balanced and Readable make clear that Job was not speaking to anyone.

source.text: וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים לְהִתְיַצֵּ֖ב עַל־יְהוָ֑ה וַיָּב֥וֹא גַֽם־הַשָּׂטָ֖ן בְּתוֹכָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was the day, and came [the] sons of God to present themselves before YHWH, and came also the satan in their midst.

en.L: And the day came when the sons of God came to present themselves before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the satan also came among them.
en.B: One day the sons of God came to present themselves before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the Accuser also came among them.
en.R: One day the heavenly beings came to stand before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and the Accuser came with them.

decisions.choice: the satan: a title, "the adversary" or "the accuser", one who opposes in a court
decisions.reason: The noun has the article, "the satan", and Hebrew does not put the article on personal names, so here it is a title or role rather than a name. The word means one who stands against someone: the LORD's angel stands in Balaam's way "as an adversary" (Numbers 22:22, 32), and in a court the satan is the accuser who stands at a man's right hand (Psalm 109:6; Zechariah 3:1-2). In Job he is one of the heavenly beings who come before the LORD, he questions Job's motives, and he can act only as far as the LORD allows (1:12; 2:6). Later Scripture uses the word as a name, Satan, for God's great enemy (1 Chronicles 21:1, without the article; Revelation 12:9), and many readers identify him with this figure. The book of Job itself does not develop that; it presents him as the accuser in the heavenly court.

decisions.choice: the sons of God: heavenly beings, members of God's council
decisions.reason: In Hebrew "son of" often means "belonging to the class of". The sons of God here are heavenly beings who serve God and gather before him as courtiers before a king, like the host of heaven standing by the LORD's throne in 1 Kings 22:19-22. Job 38:7 has them shouting for joy when the earth was founded, and Psalm 29:1 and 89:7 use a similar phrase for the heavenly beings. They are not human beings.

decisions.choice: present themselves before the LORD: come to stand before the king of heaven
decisions.reason: The verb is used of officials and servants taking their places before a ruler to report and receive orders (Zechariah 6:5, of riders who present themselves "before the Lord of all the earth"; Proverbs 22:29). The scene has moved from Job's house to the court of heaven, which Job never learns about.

decisions.choice: and it was the day: one day
decisions.reason: This is the usual Hebrew way to begin a new scene on a particular day (1:13; 2:1; 1 Samuel 1:4; 2 Kings 4:8). It does not mean a fixed festival.

decisions.choice: the satan (Literal); the Accuser (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "the satan", with the article and lowercase, to show it is a title. Balanced and Readable translate the title as "the Accuser", capitalized because it is used as his name in this story; "Satan" would make it a personal name, which the article rules out here.

decisions.choice: the heavenly beings (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Sons of God" can suggest a family of gods or human believers to a new reader. Readable says who they are; Literal and Balanced keep "the sons of God".

source.text: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֖ן מֵאַ֣יִן תָּבֹ֑א וַיַּ֨עַן הַשָּׂטָ֤ן אֶת־יְהוָה֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר מִשּׁ֣וּט בָּאָ֔רֶץ וּמֵֽהִתְהַלֵּ֖ךְ בָּֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said YHWH to the satan, from where do you come? And answered the satan YHWH and said, from roaming on the earth and from walking about on it.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to the satan, "From where do you come?" And the satan answered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "From roaming on the earth, and from walking about on it."
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to the Accuser, "Where have you come from?" The Accuser answered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "From roaming the earth and walking up and down on it."
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked the Accuser, "Where have you been?" The Accuser answered, "I have been going all over the earth, walking back and forth across it."

decisions.choice: roaming and walking about: going to and fro over the earth, as one on patrol
decisions.reason: The first verb means to go back and forth, rove; it is used of the LORD's eyes that range over all the earth (2 Chronicles 16:9; Zechariah 4:10). The second is used of the riders in Zechariah 1:10-11 whom the LORD sends "to walk about through the earth" and who report back. The satan speaks like an inspector who has been watching the earth and is ready to report.

decisions.choice: From where do you come?: the opening of a report, not a request for information
decisions.reason: The LORD's question opens the conversation, as a king asks a servant for his report; the narrator does not suggest the LORD did not know. The same exchange is repeated in 2:2.

decisions.choice: the Accuser answered (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable leaves out the repeated name of the LORD after "answered" and turns the reply into a full sentence ("I have been ..."), which is clearer for new readers.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֔ן הֲשַׂ֥מְתָּ לִבְּךָ֖ עַל־עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּ֑וֹב כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין כָּמֹ֨הוּ֙ בָּאָ֔רֶץ אִ֣ישׁ תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֥ר מֵרָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: And said YHWH to the satan, have you set your heart on my servant Job? For there is none like him on the earth, a man blameless and upright, fearing God and turning aside from evil.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to the satan, "Have you set your heart on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} slave Job? For there is none like him on the earth, a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil."
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to the Accuser, "Have you considered {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil."
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to the Accuser, "Have you noticed {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} servant Job? There is no one on earth like him. He is blameless and upright. He honors God and keeps away from evil."

decisions.choice: set your heart on: give your attention to, consider
decisions.reason: "To set the heart on" means to pay attention to something (1 Samuel 9:20; Job 34:14). Here it may also hint at watching someone closely, the satan's role as one who looks for faults; the LORD himself raises Job's name.

decisions.choice: my servant Job: one who belongs to the LORD and serves him; a title of honor
decisions.reason: The word is used of a slave or servant who belongs to a master. Spoken by the LORD of a person, it is a title of honor, given to Abraham, Moses and David (Genesis 26:24; Numbers 12:7; 2 Samuel 7:5). The LORD calls Job "my servant" again at the end of the book (42:7-8).

decisions.choice: blameless and upright ...: the LORD repeats the narrator's words of 1:1
decisions.reason: The description is word for word that of 1:1. What the narrator said, the LORD now confirms. See 1:1 for the sense of "blameless and upright".

decisions.choice: slave (Literal); servant (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As throughout the project, Literal keeps "slave" for this word so its hard edge is visible, while Balanced and Readable say "servant", which is how a title of honor is heard in English.

decisions.choice: set your heart on (Literal); considered (Balanced); noticed (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom instead of its picture.

source.text: וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה וַיֹּאמַ֑ר הַֽחִנָּ֔ם יָרֵ֥א אִיּ֖וֹב אֱלֹהִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered the satan YHWH and said, [is it] for nothing [that] fears Job God?

en.L: And the satan answered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "Is it for nothing that Job fears God?"
en.B: The Accuser answered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Does Job fear God for nothing?"
en.R: The Accuser answered {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "Does Job honor God without getting anything for it?"

decisions.choice: for nothing: without payment, with nothing to gain
decisions.reason: The word means "freely, for no pay" (Genesis 29:15, of working for nothing) and also "without cause". The satan asks whether Job's devotion is free or bought by his blessings: take the rewards away, he suggests, and the devotion will go too. This is the question the whole book tests. In 2:3 the LORD turns the same word back on him: Job was ruined "for nothing", without cause.

decisions.choice: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The question is not a request for information but a challenge: Job does not, the satan implies, fear God for nothing. The next two verses give his reasons.

decisions.choice: honor God without getting anything for it (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says "honor" as in 1:1 and spells out what "for nothing" means here.

source.text: הֲלֹֽא־אַ֠תָּה שַׂ֣כְתָּ בַעֲד֧וֹ וּבְעַד־בֵּית֛וֹ וּבְעַ֥ד כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֖וֹ מִסָּבִ֑יב מַעֲשֵׂ֤ה יָדָיו֙ בֵּרַ֔כְתָּ וּמִקְנֵ֖הוּ פָּרַ֥ץ בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: [Is it] not you [who] have put a hedge around him and around his house and around all that [is] his, round about? The work of his hands you have blessed, and his livestock has spread out in the land.

en.L: Have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not put a hedge around him and around his house and around all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his livestock has spread out in the land.
en.B: Have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not put a protective hedge around him and his household and everything he owns on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his flocks and herds have spread throughout the land.
en.R: You have put a wall of protection around him, his family and everything he owns. You have blessed everything he does, and his animals have spread all over the land.

decisions.choice: put a hedge around him: protected him on every side
decisions.reason: A hedge of thorns kept animals and thieves out of a field or vineyard (Isaiah 5:5; Proverbs 15:19). The satan means that God has shielded Job, his family and his property from all harm. Job later uses a related verb for the opposite feeling, that God has "hedged him in" (3:23).

decisions.choice: you have blessed the work of his hands: a real blessing, prosperity in all he does
decisions.reason: Here the verb "bless" has its plain sense, as in Deuteronomy 28:12 ("to bless all the work of your hand"). The satan admits Job's prosperity comes from God, and that is his complaint: the blessing explains the devotion.

decisions.choice: Have you not ...?: a question expecting the answer yes
decisions.reason: The Hebrew stresses "you": it is God himself who has protected Job. The question is a way of stating the fact.

decisions.choice: statement instead of question (Readable)
decisions.reason: The question expects "yes", so Readable states it directly, which is easier to follow.

decisions.choice: his flocks and herds have spread (Balanced); his animals (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word for livestock covers flocks and herds together (1:3); "spread out" means grown in number and spread over the land (Genesis 30:30, 43).

source.text: וְאוּלָם֙ שְֽׁלַֽח־נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ וְגַ֖ע בְּכָל־אֲשֶׁר־ל֑וֹ אִם־לֹ֥א עַל־פָּנֶ֖יךָ יְבָרֲכֶֽךָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: But stretch out, please, your hand and touch all that [is] his; if not to your face he will bless you.

en.L: But stretch out {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hand, please, and touch all that he has, [and see] if he will not curse {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} to {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} face!
en.B: But stretch out {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} hand and strike everything he has, and he will surely curse {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} to {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} face.
en.R: But reach out and take away everything he has. Then he will curse {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} to {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} face!

decisions.choice: he will curse you: the verb is "bless", meaning "curse"
decisions.reason: As in 1:5, the verb for "bless" stands in place of "curse" (see the note there). The satan's claim is that Job will turn on God openly.

decisions.choice: if he will not ...: an oath, meaning "he will surely ..."
decisions.reason: "If not" is the form of an oath whose curse is left unsaid ("may it be so to me, if he does not ..."); it makes a strong statement, "he certainly will" (Numbers 14:28). The same words return in 2:5.

decisions.choice: touch: strike, harm; to your face: openly
decisions.reason: "Touch" with God's hand means to strike with harm (Genesis 26:11; Job 19:21, "the hand of God has touched me"). "To your face" means openly, defiantly, not in secret as Job feared his children might in their hearts (1:5).

decisions.choice: reach out and take away (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says what "stretch out your hand and touch" means here: the satan asks God to take Job's possessions from him.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֗ן הִנֵּ֤ה כָל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ֙ בְּיָדֶ֔ךָ רַ֣ק אֵלָ֔יו אַל־תִּשְׁלַ֖ח יָדֶ֑ךָ וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵעִ֖ם פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said YHWH to the satan, see, all that [is] his [is] in your hand; only against him do not stretch out your hand. And went out the satan from with [the] face of YHWH.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to the satan, "Look, all that he has is in your hand; only against him do not stretch out your hand." And the satan went out from the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to the Accuser, "Very well, everything he has is in your power. Only do not lay a hand on the man himself." Then the Accuser went out from the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to the Accuser, "All right. You may do what you want with everything he has. But you must not harm Job himself." So the Accuser left the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: in your hand: in your power
decisions.reason: To be "in someone's hand" is to be under his control, to do with as he likes (Genesis 16:6; Genesis 39:4).

decisions.choice: only not against him: the satan acts only within the limit the LORD sets
decisions.reason: The satan can do nothing to Job without the LORD's permission, and the LORD sets the boundary: Job's possessions, not his body. In 2:6 the limit is moved but still kept: his body, not his life. The text does not explain why the LORD allows the test; the book leaves that question open for Job and the reader to wrestle with.

decisions.choice: went out from the presence of the LORD: left the audience
decisions.reason: "From with the face of" means from being in someone's presence, as one leaves a king's court (Genesis 4:16; 41:46). The heavenly scene closes, and the satan goes out to act.

decisions.choice: Look (Literal); Very well ... in your power (Balanced); All right. You may do what you want (Readable)
decisions.reason: The particle "see" here grants the request; Balanced and Readable render it as consent and give the sense of "in your hand".

source.text: וַיְהִ֖י הַיּ֑וֹם וּבָנָ֨יו וּבְנֹתָ֤יו אֹֽכְלִים֙ וְשֹׁתִ֣ים יַ֔יִן בְּבֵ֖ית אֲחִיהֶ֥ם הַבְּכֽוֹר׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was the day, and his sons and his daughters [were] eating and drinking wine in [the] house of their brother the firstborn.

en.L: And the day came when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother, the firstborn.
en.B: One day Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother.
en.R: One day Job's sons and daughters were having a feast at the home of their oldest brother.

decisions.choice: and it was the day: one day, the same opening as the heavenly scene
decisions.reason: The words that opened the scene in heaven (1:6) now open the scene on earth. The reader knows what has been decided; Job does not.

decisions.choice: were eating and drinking wine: a feast in progress
decisions.reason: The participles describe what was going on when the news came. It is the feast at the house of the firstborn, perhaps the first of a new round (1:4-5). The same words are repeated by the last messenger (1:18).

decisions.choice: the firstborn (Literal); oldest brother (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Firstborn" means the oldest son; Balanced and Readable say it in everyday English. Readable sums up "eating and drinking wine" as "having a feast", as in 1:4.

source.text: וּמַלְאָ֛ךְ בָּ֥א אֶל־אִיּ֖וֹב וַיֹּאמַ֑ר הַבָּקָר֙ הָי֣וּ חֹֽרְשׁ֔וֹת וְהָאֲתֹנ֖וֹת רֹע֥וֹת עַל־יְדֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And a messenger came to Job and said, the oxen were plowing and the female donkeys grazing beside them,

en.L: And a messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing, and the female donkeys were grazing beside them,
en.B: A messenger came to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them,
en.R: A messenger came to Job and said, "Your oxen were plowing in the field, and your donkeys were eating grass nearby.

decisions.choice: beside them: literally "on their hands"
decisions.reason: "On the hands of" means at the side of, next to (Judges 11:26; Numbers 2:17 in a similar sense). The donkeys were grazing near the plowing oxen; both were taken in one raid.

decisions.choice: a messenger: a human servant bringing news
decisions.reason: The word means one who is sent, and can mean an angel (a messenger of God), but here it is plainly one of Job's servants who escaped (1:15).

decisions.choice: your oxen, your donkeys; in the field (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable adds "your" and "in the field", which the scene implies, and ends the sentence here; Literal and Balanced end with a comma because the report runs on into the next verse.

source.text: וַתִּפֹּ֤ל שְׁבָא֙ וַתִּקָּחֵ֔ם וְאֶת־הַנְּעָרִ֖ים הִכּ֣וּ לְפִי־חָ֑רֶב וָֽאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: and fell Sheba and took them, and the servants they struck to [the] mouth of [the] sword, and escaped only I alone to tell you.

en.L: and Sheba fell [on them] and took them, and they struck down the young men with the edge of the sword; and I alone have escaped to tell you."
en.B: when the Sabeans swept down and carried them off. They killed the servants with the sword, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you."
en.R: Then the Sabeans attacked and took the animals away. They killed your servants with their swords. I am the only one who got away to tell you."

decisions.choice: Sheba: the Sabeans, a people of Arabia, here as raiders
decisions.reason: Sheba was a people of Arabia known for trade caravans (6:19; 1 Kings 10:1-2; Ezekiel 27:22). The name stands for the people, with a singular verb, "Sheba fell on them". Here they come as raiders from the desert.

decisions.choice: the young men: Job's servants
decisions.reason: The word means young men, and is often used of servants, as here the herdsmen and plowmen. In 1:19 the same word refers to Job's sons and daughters.

decisions.choice: with the edge of the sword: literally "to the mouth of the sword"
decisions.reason: The sword is pictured as a mouth that devours (Genesis 34:26; Joshua 6:21). The phrase means they were killed without mercy.

decisions.choice: I alone have escaped to tell you: the refrain of the four reports
decisions.reason: Each messenger ends with the same words (1:15, 16, 17, 19), and each arrives while the last is still speaking. The repetition gives the effect of blow after blow with no time to take in one loss before the next. The servant who survives exists only to carry the news.

decisions.choice: the young men (Literal); the servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the word's literal sense; Balanced and Readable say who they were.

source.text: ע֣וֹד׀זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֗ר וְזֶה֮ בָּ֣א וַיֹּאמַר֒ אֵ֣שׁ אֱלֹהִ֗ים נָֽפְלָה֙ מִן־הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַתִּבְעַ֥ר בַּצֹּ֛אן וּבַנְּעָרִ֖ים וַתֹּאכְלֵ֑ם וָאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: Still this [one was] speaking, and this [one] came and said, [the] fire of God fell from the heavens and burned the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and escaped only I alone to tell you.

en.L: While this one was still speaking, another came and said, "The fire of God fell from the heavens and burned up the sheep and the young men and consumed them; and I alone have escaped to tell you."
en.B: While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "The fire of God fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them. I am the only one who has escaped to tell you."
en.R: He was still speaking when another messenger arrived and said, "Fire from God fell from the sky and burned up your sheep and your servants. I am the only one who got away to tell you."

decisions.choice: the fire of God: fire from the sky, probably lightning, seen as sent by God
decisions.reason: Fire falling from the heavens is most likely lightning, which was seen as God's own fire (2 Kings 1:12, "the fire of God came down from heaven"; Numbers 11:1). The messenger takes it as God's act. The reader knows that the satan brought it with the LORD's permission (1:12).

decisions.choice: still this one speaking, and this one came: one messenger after another
decisions.reason: Hebrew uses "this ... this" for "one ... another". The second arrives before the first has finished.

decisions.choice: I alone have escaped to tell you: the refrain of the four reports
decisions.reason: Each messenger ends with the same words (1:15, 16, 17, 19), and each arrives while the last is still speaking. The repetition gives the effect of blow after blow with no time to take in one loss before the next. The servant who survives exists only to carry the news.

decisions.choice: the young men (Literal); the servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1:15.

source.text: ע֣וֹד׀זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֗ר וְזֶה֮ בָּ֣א וַיֹּאמַר֒ כַּשְׂדִּ֞ים שָׂ֣מוּ׀שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה רָאשִׁ֗ים וַֽיִּפְשְׁט֤וּ עַל־הַגְּמַלִּים֙ וַיִּקָּח֔וּם וְאֶת־הַנְּעָרִ֖ים הִכּ֣וּ לְפִי־חָ֑רֶב וָאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: Still this [one was] speaking, and this [one] came and said, [the] Chaldeans formed three companies and made a raid on the camels and took them, and the servants they struck to [the] mouth of [the] sword, and escaped only I alone to tell you.

en.L: While this one was still speaking, another came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three bands and made a raid on the camels and took them, and they struck down the young men with the edge of the sword; and I alone have escaped to tell you."
en.B: While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "The Chaldeans formed three raiding parties, swept down on the camels and carried them off. They killed the servants with the sword, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you."
en.R: He was still speaking when another messenger arrived and said, "Three groups of Chaldean raiders attacked your camels and took them away. They killed your servants with their swords. I am the only one who got away to tell you."

decisions.choice: the Chaldeans: tribes of the land along the lower Euphrates, here as raiders
decisions.reason: The Chaldeans are the people of southern Mesopotamia (Genesis 11:28, "Ur of the Chaldeans"), who later ruled Babylon. Here they appear as raiding bands from the desert to the east, not as an empire. The four disasters alternate: raiders (1:15), fire from the sky (1:16), raiders (1:17), wind (1:19).

decisions.choice: formed three companies: split into three groups
decisions.reason: "Heads" here means divisions of an armed band (Judges 7:16; 9:43; 1 Samuel 11:11). Attacking from three sides was a way to surround and take a large herd.

decisions.choice: I alone have escaped to tell you: the refrain of the four reports
decisions.reason: Each messenger ends with the same words (1:15, 16, 17, 19), and each arrives while the last is still speaking. The repetition gives the effect of blow after blow with no time to take in one loss before the next. The servant who survives exists only to carry the news.

decisions.choice: the young men (Literal); the servants (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1:15.

source.text: עַ֚ד זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֔ר וְזֶ֖ה בָּ֣א וַיֹּאמַ֑ר בָּנֶ֨יךָ וּבְנוֹתֶ֤יךָ אֹֽכְלִים֙ וְשֹׁתִ֣ים יַ֔יִן בְּבֵ֖ית אֲחִיהֶ֥ם הַבְּכֽוֹר׃

records.literal_gloss: While this [one was] speaking, and this [one] came and said, your sons and your daughters [were] eating and drinking wine in [the] house of their brother the firstborn,

en.L: While this one was speaking, another came and said, "Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother, the firstborn,
en.B: While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother,
en.R: He was still speaking when another messenger arrived and said, "Your sons and daughters were having a feast at the home of their oldest brother.

decisions.choice: while: a different word from verses 16-17, with the same sense
decisions.reason: Verses 16 and 17 begin "still"; this verse begins with a word that usually means "until" but here means "while" (as in 1 Samuel 14:19 in a similar sense). The meaning is the same: the fourth messenger interrupts the third.

decisions.choice: your sons and your daughters were eating ...: the words of 1:13 repeated
decisions.reason: The messenger repeats the narrator's words from 1:13 almost exactly, so the reader recognizes the scene and knows what is coming before Job hears it.

decisions.choice: the firstborn (Literal); oldest brother (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: As in 1:13. Literal and Balanced end with a comma because the report continues into the next verse.

source.text: וְהִנֵּה֩ ר֨וּחַ גְּדוֹלָ֜ה בָּ֣אָה׀מֵעֵ֣בֶר הַמִּדְבָּ֗ר וַיִּגַּע֙ בְּאַרְבַּע֙ פִּנּ֣וֹת הַבַּ֔יִת וַיִּפֹּ֥ל עַל־הַנְּעָרִ֖ים וַיָּמ֑וּתוּ וָאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק־אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: and see, a wind great came from across the wilderness and struck [the] four corners of the house, and it fell on the young people and they died, and escaped only I alone to tell you.

en.L: and look, a great wind came from across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young people, and they died; and I alone have escaped to tell you."
en.B: when suddenly a great wind came from across the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It fell on the young people, and they are dead. I am the only one who has escaped to tell you."
en.R: Suddenly a powerful wind blew in from the desert and hit all four corners of the house. The house fell on your children, and they are dead. I am the only one who got away to tell you."

decisions.choice: the young people: Job's sons and daughters
decisions.reason: The word is the same as "young men" in 1:15-17, but here it refers to those eating in the house, Job's children (1:18). Its masculine plural form covers the daughters too.

decisions.choice: a great wind from across the wilderness striking the four corners: a desert storm
decisions.reason: Violent winds came in from the desert east of the settled land (Jeremiah 4:11; 13:24; Hosea 13:15). A wind that strikes all four corners at once is a whirlwind, which brought the whole house down.

decisions.choice: struck: the same verb as "touch" in 1:11
decisions.reason: The wind "touched" the house: the same verb the satan used when he asked God to "touch" all Job had (1:11). The reader sees the request carried out.

decisions.choice: I alone have escaped to tell you: the refrain of the four reports
decisions.reason: Each messenger ends with the same words (1:15, 16, 17, 19), and each arrives while the last is still speaking. The repetition gives the effect of blow after blow with no time to take in one loss before the next. The servant who survives exists only to carry the news.

decisions.choice: the young people (Literal, Balanced); your children (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who died.

source.text: וַיָּ֤קָם אִיּוֹב֙ וַיִּקְרַ֣ע אֶת־מְעִל֔וֹ וַיָּ֖גָז אֶת־רֹאשׁ֑וֹ וַיִּפֹּ֥ל אַ֖רְצָה וַיִּשְׁתָּֽחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And arose Job and tore his robe and shaved his head, and fell to the ground and worshiped.

en.L: And Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head, and he fell to the ground and worshiped.
en.B: Then Job got up, tore his robe and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped.
en.R: Then Job stood up. He tore his robe and shaved his head to show his grief. Then he bowed down with his face to the ground and worshiped God.

decisions.choice: tore his robe and shaved his head: signs of mourning
decisions.reason: Tearing one's clothes and shaving the head were ways of showing grief at a death or disaster (Genesis 37:34; Jeremiah 41:5; Micah 1:16). The robe was the outer garment worn by a man of rank.

decisions.choice: fell to the ground and worshiped: bowed face down before God
decisions.reason: The verb means to bow low, often lying face down, before a king or before God; it is the usual word for worship. The satan expected Job to curse God (1:11); instead he worships.

decisions.choice: to show his grief; worshiped God (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says why Job tore his robe and shaved his head, which a new reader may not know, and names God as the one he worshiped, which the verse implies.

source.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ עָרֹ֨ם יָצָ֜אתִי מִבֶּ֣טֶן אִמִּ֗י וְעָרֹם֙ אָשׁ֣וּב שָׁ֔מָהיְהוָ֣ה נָתַ֔ן וַיהוָ֖ה לָקָ֑ח יְהִ֛י שֵׁ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה מְבֹרָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, naked I came out from [the] womb of my mother, and naked I will return there; YHWH gave and YHWH has taken; may be [the] name of YHWH blessed.

en.L: And he said, "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, \q and naked I will return there. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} gave, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has taken; \q may the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be blessed."
en.B: He said, "I came naked from my mother's womb, \q and naked I will go back there. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} gave, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has taken away; \q may the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be blessed."
en.R: He said, "I had nothing when I was born, \q and I will have nothing when I die. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} gave, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has taken away. \q May the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be praised!"

decisions.choice: naked I will return there: I will leave the world with nothing, as I came
alternatives: return to the womb of the earth
decisions.reason: Job pictures his birth and his death as two journeys with nothing in his hands (Ecclesiastes 5:14, numbered 5:15 in many Bibles, uses the same picture). "There" cannot mean his mother's womb; it is most likely the earth, from which human beings were taken and to which they return (Genesis 3:19), pictured as a mother's womb (Psalm 139:15). The point is that everything he lost was given, not owned.

decisions.choice: the LORD gave and the LORD has taken: Job sees the LORD's hand behind his losses
decisions.reason: Job does not blame raiders, fire or wind but traces both his blessings and his losses to the LORD, and the narrator approves (1:22). He does not know of the satan's part, and the book never tells him. Here Job uses the divine name, which in the speeches of the book is rare (12:9).

decisions.choice: may the name of the LORD be blessed: real blessing, praise
decisions.reason: The verb is the one the satan said Job would use as a curse (1:11). Job uses it in its true sense: he praises the LORD. The "name" stands for the LORD himself as he is known.

decisions.choice: set in four lines
decisions.reason: The saying has the balance of Hebrew poetry: two lines on birth and death, two on the LORD's giving and taking. The lines follow the verse's Hebrew accents (the main division after "has taken", lesser ones after "my mother's womb" and "there"). The rest of chapters 1-2 is prose.

decisions.choice: I had nothing when I was born ... when I die; praised (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of nakedness and of returning "there". It says "praised" for the verb here so that it is not confused with "blessed" in the sense of being given good things.

source.text: בְּכָל־זֹ֖את לֹא־חָטָ֣א אִיּ֑וֹב וְלֹא־נָתַ֥ן תִּפְלָ֖ה לֵאלֹהִֽים׃פ

records.literal_gloss: In all this not sinned Job, and not he ascribed wrongdoing to God.

en.L: In all this Job did not sin, and he did not ascribe anything unseemly to God.
en.B: In all this Job did not sin or accuse God of wrongdoing.
en.R: Even after all this, Job did not sin. He did not blame God for doing anything wrong.

decisions.choice: did not ascribe anything unseemly to God: did not accuse God of wrong
alternatives: did not charge God with folly
decisions.reason: The rare noun means something unseemly or offensive, what is morally tasteless (24:12; Jeremiah 23:13). "To give" it to God means to say that God acted improperly. Job grieves, but he does not accuse God.

decisions.choice: in all this Job did not sin: the narrator's verdict on the first test
decisions.reason: The narrator answers the satan's prediction (1:11): Job did not curse God. A similar verdict closes the second test (2:10).

decisions.choice: anything unseemly (Literal); wrongdoing (Balanced); anything wrong (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the sense of what is improper; Balanced and Readable say what the phrase amounts to.
